# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

## Overview

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
3. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
4. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
5. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
6. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill";
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**
- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**
- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**
- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

## After the Design

**Documentation:**
- Write the validated design to `docs/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Implementation:**
- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

1→# DuckDB Data Agent
     2→
     3→> **Note:** This project is built with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code)(using Opus 4.6 and [superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers)) by **more than 99%** and human-reviewed by author.
     4→
     5→https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/32066f7d-a6b8-41bc-bde2-c85a19cf2e8c
     6→
     7→Or you can see examples online: [example1](https://raw.githack.com/cyyeh/duckdb-data-agent/main/examples/example1.html), [example2](https://raw.githack.com/cyyeh/duckdb-data-agent/main/examples/example2.html), [example3](https://raw.githack.com/cyyeh/duckdb-data-agent/main/examples/example3.html), [example4](https://raw.githack.com/cyyeh/duckdb-data-agent/main/examples/example4.html), [example5](https://raw.githack.com/cyyeh/duckdb-data-agent/main/examples/example5.html)
     8→
     9→---
    10→
    11→An AI-powered data analysis agent with a built-in SQL playground. Upload data files (CSV, JSON, Parquet, Excel) and ask questions in plain English — the agent delegates to a specialized subagent for SQL queries and renders charts inline — or switch to the SQL editor for direct queries. Powered by [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) on a lightweight [FastAPI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/) backend with a React frontend. The app opens in Agent Mode by default so you can start analyzing data immediately.
    12→
    13→Each browser tab gets its own isolated DuckDB session — uploaded data and query state are fully isolated between users and tabs. Sessions are persisted to disk so your tables survive idle timeouts; the session file is only deleted when you close the tab explicitly.
    14→
    15→## Features
    16→
    17→### General
    18→
    19→- **Per-user DuckDB sessions** — Each browser tab gets its own isolated DuckDB instance, identified by a `X-Session-ID` header generated client-side; data and state are never shared between users or tabs; sessions are persisted to disk (`/tmp/duckdb-data-agent-{session_id}.duckdb`) so tables survive idle timeouts and reconnections; the session file is deleted only on explicit tab close
    20→- **DuckDB SQL engine** — Fast, in-process analytical database on the backend
    21→- **Multi-format file upload** — Drag-and-drop or click to import CSV, JSON, Parquet, and Excel (.xlsx) files (default limit: 500 MB, configurable via `MAX_TOTAL_SIZE_BYTES` env var) with automatic schema detection; Excel workbooks with multiple sheets create one table per sheet; duplicate filename detection prevents accidental overwrites; the upload UI appears when no tables are loaded, and files can also be added via the sidebar upload button
    22→- **Sample dataset** — One-click load of the Titanic dataset to get started quickly
    23→- **Table sidebar** — Collapsible panel to browse tables, inspect columns, and view types
    24→- **Dark / light mode** — Toggle between dark and light themes with the sun/moon button in the header; respects your OS preference on first visit and remembers your choice across sessions
    25→- **Internationalization (i18n)** — Switch between English and Traditional Chinese with the EN/中 toggle in the header; auto-detects your OS language on first visit and remembers your choice across sessions
    26→- **Interactive clarification** — When your request is ambiguous, the agent asks a clarifying question with selectable options displayed inline in the chat; pick an option or type a free-text response to continue
    27→- **Export conversation** — Click the Export button to download the full conversation as a single self-contained HTML file; the export preserves the current theme, collapsible thinking blocks, interactive Plotly charts (via CDN), and styled query result tables; interactive-only elements (edit/delete buttons, retry buttons) are stripped for a clean read-only view
    28→- **Conversation history** — The bottom half of the sidebar lists past conversations for the current browser tab, ordered by most recent; click to reload a previous conversation, rename it inline, or delete it; conversations are scoped to the browser tab's session and automatically cleaned up when the tab is closed; backed by a SQLite database for durability within a session; a new conversation is created automatically when you send the first message
    29→
    30→### Agent Mode (default mode)
    31→
    32→- **Natural language queries** — Ask questions about your data in plain English; the orchestrator delegates to specialized subagents that write and execute SQL for you
    33→- **Subagent architecture** — An orchestrator agent delegates to a **sql-analyst** subagent for data queries, with a configurable model (via `SQL_SUBAGENT_MODEL` env var, defaulting to `haiku`); the orchestrator itself handles chart rendering via `render_chart` for coherent interleaved text-and-chart answers
    34→- **Streaming responses** — Real-time token streaming powered by Claude via the [Anthropic Agent SDK](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python); subagent internal reasoning is filtered from the main stream
    35→- **Live cross-conversation streaming** — Start a query in one conversation, switch to another, and both streams run concurrently; a pulsing dot in the sidebar indicates which conversations are actively streaming; switch back to a streaming conversation for instant re-attachment with no lost tokens
    36→- **Visible reasoning** — Collapsible thinking block shows the agent's intermediate steps and SQL queries
    37→- **Inline results** — Query results rendered inline within the conversation
    38→- **Chart generation** — Ask for a chart or visualization and the orchestrator generates it inline; supports bar, scatter, line, pie, histogram, box, and heatmap chart types with optional multi-series grouping; animated charts with frames, sliders, and play/pause controls are also supported
    39→- **Dual chart library support** — Toggle between [Plotly](https://plotly.com/javascript/) and [Vega-Lite](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/) chart renderers via a toggle button in the agent panel header; the selected library is persisted to localStorage and sent to the backend so the agent emits native chart specs for the chosen library; defaults to Plotly for backward compatibility
    40→- **Response time** — Each answer block shows the agent response time (e.g., "Answered in 3.2s") after streaming completes, giving visibility into query latency
    41→- **Edit & delete messages** — Hover over any user message to edit or delete it; editing re-sends the modified query with prior conversation as context, deleting rewinds the conversation to that point
    42→- **Bifrost LLM gateway** — A [Bifrost](https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost) gateway service manages API keys centrally and routes LLM requests to multiple providers; sidecar containers never have access to real API keys (see [Security](#security))
    43→- **Privacy-conscious** — Requires an Anthropic API key stored in a server-side `.env` file; your data and credentials are never sent anywhere besides the Anthropic API
    44→- **Container isolation** — Run each agent session inside a [gVisor](https://gvisor.dev/)-sandboxed Docker container for code execution sandboxing and multi-tenant isolation; read-only rootfs, all capabilities dropped, no host filesystem or Docker socket access (see [Container Isolation](#container-isolation))
    45→- **Langfuse observability** (optional) — Built-in [Langfuse](https://langfuse.com/) tracing for monitoring agent interactions
    46→
    47→### Editor Mode
    48→
    49→- **SQL query editor** — Write and execute queries with Ctrl/Cmd+Enter
    50→- **Interactive results** — Sortable columns, per-column filters, and global search across results
    51→- **EXPLAIN support** — Markdown-rendered output for `EXPLAIN` and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` queries
    52→
    53→### Memories
    54→
    55→- **Persistent agent memory** — The agent remembers facts, preferences, and patterns across conversations; memories are stored as markdown files on disk (`data/memories/{user_id}/MEMORY.md`) and injected into the system prompt at the start of each conversation, with stored user preferences taking priority over default model behaviors
    56→- **MCP-based memory tools** — The agent saves, recalls, and forgets memories via MCP tools (`save_memory`, `recall_memories`, `forget_memory`); duplicate detection prevents storing the same memory twice
    57→- **Memory management UI** — A Memories tab in the sidebar lets you view and delete individual memories; a file icon button opens a detail modal showing the full `MEMORY.md` file with Preview (rendered markdown) and Source (raw text) tabs, matching the skill detail modal
    58→
    59→### Skills
    60→
    61→- **Browse skills** — A "Skills" tab in the sidebar lists available skills with name and description; click a skill to open a detail modal with Preview and Source tabs; click "Use" to append a `/skill-name` slash command to the current chat input text
    62→- **Invoke skills via slash command** — Type `/` anywhere in the chat input to open an autocomplete dropdown of available skills; the menu filters as you type and works at any cursor position, not just the beginning of the input
    63→- **Multiple skills per message** — Combine multiple skills in a single message (e.g., `use this skill /analyze-data use this skill /my-other-skill What is the average revenue?`); all referenced skills are invoked before the agent processes your question
    64→- **Enable/disable skills** — Toggle the eye icon on any skill to enable or disable it; disabled skills are hidden from the slash command menu and cannot be invoked
    65→- **Delete skills** — Remove custom skills via the delete button in the sidebar; built-in skills (like `analyze-data`) cannot be deleted
    66→- **Create skills from the UI** — Click the "+" button in the Skills tab to create a new skill with a name, description, and step-by-step instructions; skills are stored as `SKILL.md` files on disk
    67→- **Agent-created skills** — The agent can create new skills during a conversation via the `create_skill` MCP tool; new skills appear in the sidebar automatically
    68→- **Dynamic skill discovery** — Skills are stored at `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and re-scanned per request; add or remove skills without restarting
    69→
    70→### Plugins
    71→
    72→- **Data analysis plugin** — The [knowledge-work-plugins/data](https://github.com/anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins/tree/main/data) plugin is bundled at `plugins/data/`, providing specialized commands and skills for data work
    73→- **Plugin commands** — Invoke via slash commands: `/data:analyze`, `/data:explore-data`, `/data:write-query`, `/data:create-viz`, `/data:build-dashboard`, `/data:validate`
    74→- **Plugin skills** — The plugin adds skills for SQL queries, data exploration, data visualization, statistical analysis, data validation, interactive dashboard building, and data context extraction
    75→- **Plugin isolation** — Plugins are bind-mounted read-only into sidecar containers at `/app/plugins/`; the plugin's external MCP server connections (Snowflake, Databricks, etc.) are neutralized since the agent uses its own DuckDB MCP server
    76→- **Dashboard limitation** — The `/data:build-dashboard` command can generate HTML dashboards inside the sidecar container, but the output is **not yet visible** in the UI; the sidecar writes to ephemeral tmpfs storage that is inaccessible from the browser, and the frontend has no HTML preview or iframe rendering support; see [`docs/plans/2026-03-03-inline-dashboard-rendering.md`](docs/plans/2026-03-03-inline-dashboard-rendering.md) for the implementation plan to add inline dashboard rendering via a `render_dashboard` MCP tool
    77→

    79→

    85→- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/)

# Agent-Sandbox Example Overview

## Purpose & Functionality

This example demonstrates executing commands within isolated Kubernetes-based sandboxes using the OpenSandbox Python SDK. It specifically: "creates a sandbox backed by `kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox` and executes `echo hello world`" to show basic sandbox functionality for AI agent workloads.

## Architecture & Integration

The system uses a multi-layered approach:

- **Kubernetes Runtime**: OpenSandbox server operates on Kubernetes clusters
- **Agent-Sandbox Controller**: Manages sandbox lifecycle via custom Kubernetes resources
- **Execd Image**: `opensandbox/execd:v1.0.6` handles command execution
- **Shutdown Policy**: Configured to delete resources after sandbox completion

This architecture enables AI agents to safely execute arbitrary commands in isolated environments without affecting the host system.

## Setup Requirements

Prerequisites include:
- Kubernetes cluster with agent-sandbox controller and CRDs installed
- OpenSandbox server with Kubernetes runtime configured
- Container image with bash support (example uses Ubuntu 22.04)

## Configuration

Key settings in `~/.sandbox.toml`:

```toml
[runtime]
type = "kubernetes"
execd_image = "opensandbox/execd:v1.0.6"

[kubernetes]
namespace = "default"
workload_provider = "agent-sandbox"

[agent_sandbox]
shutdown_policy = "Delete"
```

## Usage Pattern

Installation and execution:
```bash
uv pip install opensandbox
uv run python examples/agent-sandbox/main.py
```

Expected output: `command output: hello world`

This demonstrates basic sandbox invocation suitable for AI agent task execution scenarios.

# OpenSandbox: Comprehensive Overview

## What is OpenSandbox?

OpenSandbox is described as a "general-purpose sandbox platform for AI applications" offering multi-language SDKs, unified sandbox APIs, and container runtimes. It enables isolated execution environments for coding agents, GUI automation, agent evaluation, code execution, and reinforcement learning workloads.

## Core Architecture

The platform comprises several interconnected components:

- **Server**: A Python FastAPI-based lifecycle management service
- **Execution Daemon (execd)**: Handles command execution and file operations within sandboxes
- **Ingress Gateway**: Manages inbound traffic with multiple routing strategies
- **Egress Controller**: Implements per-sandbox network policies
- **Runtime Orchestration**: Supports both Docker and Kubernetes backends

## Multi-Language SDK Support

OpenSandbox provides SDKs across major programming languages:
- Python
- Java/Kotlin
- JavaScript/TypeScript
- C#/.NET
- Go (roadmap)

Each SDK includes two layers: a base sandbox SDK (lifecycle, commands, file operations) and a specialized Code Interpreter SDK.

## Deployment Options

**Docker**: Local deployment using Docker containers with automatic lifecycle management.

**Kubernetes**: "High-performance Kubernetes runtime" enabling distributed scheduling and large-scale deployment.

## Key Features

The platform offers built-in implementations for:
- Command execution environments
- Filesystem operations
- Code interpreter functionality
- Examples spanning Chrome/Playwright automation, VS Code integration, and desktop environments with VNC access

## Configuration & APIs

OpenSandbox defines standardized APIs through OpenAPI specifications covering:
- Sandbox lifecycle operations
- Code execution protocols
- Network ingress/egress policies

The server configuration is TOML-based, with example configurations provided for Docker deployments.

## Open Source Status

Licensed under Apache 2.0, the project includes 591 commits with active development. The repository contains comprehensive examples demonstrating integration with Claude Code, Google Gemini, and other AI coding agents.

     4→from dataclasses import dataclass, field
     5→from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
     6→
     7→from app.database import Database

     9→logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
    10→
    11→
    12→@dataclass
    13→class SessionEntry:
    14→    db: Database
    15→    last_seen_at: datetime = field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    16→
    17→
    18→class SessionManager:
    19→    def __init__(self) -> None:
    20→        self._sessions: dict[str, SessionEntry] = {}
    21→        self._lock = threading.Lock()
    22→
    23→    def get_or_create(self, session_id: str) -> Database:
    24→        with self._lock:
    25→            if session_id not in self._sessions:
    26→                logger.info("Creating new session: %s", session_id)
    27→                db_path = f"/tmp/duckdb-data-agent-{session_id}.duckdb"
    28→                self._sessions[session_id] = SessionEntry(db=Database(db_path))
    29→            else:
    30→                self._sessions[session_id].last_seen_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    31→            return self._sessions[session_id].db
    32→
    33→    def touch(self, session_id: str) -> bool:
    34→        with self._lock:
    35→            if session_id not in self._sessions:
    36→                return False
    37→            self._sessions[session_id].last_seen_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    38→            return True
    39→
    40→    def destroy(self, session_id: str, delete_file: bool = True) -> None:
    41→        with self._lock:
    42→            entry = self._sessions.pop(session_id, None)
    43→        if entry is None:
    44→            return
    45→        db_path = entry.db.db_path
    46→        try:
    47→            entry.db.conn.close()
    48→        except Exception:
    49→            pass
    50→        if delete_file and db_path != ":memory:":
    51→            for path in [db_path, db_path + ".wal"]:
    52→                try:
    53→                    os.remove(path)
    54→                except FileNotFoundError:
    55→                    pass
    56→        logger.info("Destroyed session: %s (delete_file=%s)", session_id, delete_file)
    57→
    58→    def cleanup_stale(self, ttl_seconds: int = 300) -> list[str]:
    59→        cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(seconds=ttl_seconds)
    60→        with self._lock:
    61→            stale = [
    62→                sid for sid, entry in self._sessions.items()
    63→                if entry.last_seen_at < cutoff
    64→            ]
    65→        for sid in stale:
    66→            self.destroy(sid, delete_file=False)
    67→        return stale
    68→

     8→from app.config import MODEL_REWRITES, DEFAULT_TOOL_MODEL, BIFROST_BASE_URL

    10→logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
    11→
    12→ANTHROPIC_UPSTREAM = BIFROST_BASE_URL + "/anthropic"
    13→
    14→_SKIP_REQUEST_HEADERS = {
    15→    "host", "content-length", "transfer-encoding", "connection",
    16→}
    17→_SKIP_RESPONSE_HEADERS = {"transfer-encoding", "content-encoding", "connection"}
    18→
    19→router = APIRouter(prefix="/anthropic")
    20→
    21→
    22→def rewrite_model_in_body(
    23→    body: bytes, rewrites: dict[str, str], fallback: str = ""
    24→) -> bytes:
    25→    """Rewrite the 'model' field in a JSON body using the rewrites map.
    26→
    27→    Matches if the model string equals or contains a rewrite key
    28→    (e.g. 'sonnet' matches 'claude-sonnet-4-6').
    29→    If no rewrite matches and a fallback is set, rewrites to the fallback.
    30→    Returns the body unchanged if no match/fallback or if body is not valid JSON.
    31→    """
    32→    if not rewrites and not fallback:
    33→        return body
    34→    try:
    35→        data = json.loads(body)
    36→    except (json.JSONDecodeError, UnicodeDecodeError):
    37→        return body
    38→    model = data.get("model")
    39→    if not model or not isinstance(model, str):
    40→        return body
    41→    for tier, real_model in rewrites.items():
    42→        if model == tier or tier in model:
    43→            data["model"] = real_model
    44→            return json.dumps(data).encode()
    45→    if fallback:
    46→        data["model"] = fallback
    47→        return json.dumps(data).encode()
    48→    return body
    49→
    50→
    51→@router.api_route("/{path:path}", methods=["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "PATCH"])
    52→async def proxy_to_upstream(path: str, request: Request):
    53→    headers = {
    54→        k: v for k, v in request.headers.items()
    55→        if k.lower() not in _SKIP_REQUEST_HEADERS
    56→    }
    57→
    58→    body = await request.body()
    59→
    60→    # Rewrite model on POST requests (messages, completions, etc.)
    61→    if request.method == "POST" and (MODEL_REWRITES or DEFAULT_TOOL_MODEL):
    62→        body = rewrite_model_in_body(body, MODEL_REWRITES, fallback=DEFAULT_TOOL_MODEL)
    63→
    64→    client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=httpx.Timeout(300.0))
    65→    try:
    66→        upstream_req = client.build_request(
    67→            method=request.method,
    68→            url=f"{ANTHROPIC_UPSTREAM}/{path}",
    69→            headers=headers,
    70→            content=body,
    71→        )
    72→        upstream_resp = await client.send(upstream_req, stream=True)
    73→
    74→        response_headers = {
    75→            k: v for k, v in upstream_resp.headers.items()
    76→            if k.lower() not in _SKIP_RESPONSE_HEADERS
    77→        }
    78→
    79→        # For error responses, read the full body and log it so we can
    80→        # debug upstream failures (e.g. Anthropic API 400 errors).
    81→        if upstream_resp.status_code >= 400:

    83→            await upstream_resp.aclose()
    84→            await client.aclose()
    85→            # Extract model from request for context

    93→                f"[proxy] {upstream_resp.status_code} {request.method} /{path}"
    94→                f" model={req_model}:"
    95→                f" {error_body.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')[:2000]}",
    96→                flush=True,
    97→            )
    98→            return Response(
    99→                content=error_body,

   101→                headers=response_headers,
   102→            )
   103→
   104→        async def body_generator():

   107→                    yield chunk
   108→            finally:
   109→                await upstream_resp.aclose()

   111→
   112→        return StreamingResponse(

   115→            headers=response_headers,

   117→    except Exception:

    sandbox = await Sandbox.create(
        image,
        connection_config=config,
        timeout=timedelta(minutes=10),
    )

    async with sandbox:
        execution = await sandbox.commands.run("echo hello world")
        stdout = execution.logs.stdout[0].text if execution.logs.stdout else ""
        print(f"command output: {stdout}")
        await sandbox.kill()


if __name__ == "__main__":

## Overview
OpenSandbox is a "general-purpose sandbox platform for AI applications" offering multi-language SDKs, unified APIs, and Docker/Kubernetes runtimes for coding agents, GUI agents, and AI code execution.

- **Multi-language SDKs**: Python, Java/Kotlin, JavaScript/TypeScript, C#/.NET, with Go roadmapped
- **Sandbox Protocol**: Lifecycle management and execution APIs for custom runtime extensions
- **Runtime Support**: Docker and high-performance Kubernetes implementations for local and distributed deployment
- **Built-in Environments**: Command execution, filesystem operations, code interpreter with examples for Chrome, Playwright, VS Code, and desktop environments
- **Network Control**: Unified Ingress Gateway with routing strategies plus per-sandbox egress management

uv pip install opensandbox-server

- Code interpreter instantiation

# OpenSandbox Architecture Overview

OpenSandbox is a universal sandbox platform with four main layers:

## Architecture Layers

**1. SDKs Layer** - Client libraries (Python, Java/Kotlin, TypeScript roadmap) providing high-level abstractions for sandbox interaction.

**2. Specs Layer** - OpenAPI specifications defining two core protocols:
- Sandbox Lifecycle Spec: Create, list, get, delete, pause, resume, renew, and manage sandbox endpoints
- Sandbox Execution Spec (execd API): Code execution, commands, filesystem operations, and metrics

**3. Runtime Layer** - Server implementations managing lifecycle:
- Docker Runtime (production-ready) with host/bridge networking modes
- Kubernetes Runtime (roadmap)
- Custom runtime support via pluggable architecture

**4. Sandbox Instances Layer** - Running containers with injected execd daemon

## Core Components

**execd Daemon** - Go-based HTTP service (Beego framework) running inside each sandbox responsible for:
- Multi-language code execution via Jupyter kernel integration
- Shell command execution with streaming output
- File operations (CRUD, bulk operations, search, permissions)
- System metrics collection

**Container Structure:**
- Base container (user-specified image)
- Injected execd binary
- User entrypoint process

## Communication Flows

**Sandbox Creation:**
1. SDK sends creation request to lifecycle API
2. Runtime pulls image, injects execd, creates container
3. Container starts: Jupyter Server → execd daemon → user entrypoint

**Code Execution:**
SDKs → execd API → Jupyter runtime → kernel execution → SSE streaming back to client

**File Operations:**
Multi-part uploads/downloads routed through execd to container filesystem

## Key Design Principles

- **Protocol-first**: All interactions defined by OpenAPI specs enabling polyglot implementations
- **Separation of concerns**: Distinct responsibilities across SDK, specs, runtime, and execd layers
- **Extensibility**: Pluggable runtimes, custom images, multiple Jupyter kernels
- **Security**: API/token authentication, isolated environments, resource quotas, network isolation options
- **Observability**: Structured state transitions, real-time metrics, health checks

## Notable Features

- Stateful code execution across multiple languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Bash)
- Dynamic injection mechanism (no image modification required)
- Automatic TTL management with renewal support
- Real-time output streaming via Server-Sent Events
- Support for AI-generated code execution, interactive notebooks, testing, and remote development

# OpenSandbox API Specification Summary

## Overview

OpenSandbox provides two primary APIs for sandbox management and code execution. Base URLs: `http://localhost:8080/v1` (lifecycle) and `http://localhost:8080` (execd).

## Sandbox Lifecycle API

**Authentication:** `OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY` header or `OPEN_SANDBOX_API_KEY` environment variable

### Core Endpoints

| Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
|--------|----------|---------|
| POST | `/sandboxes` | Create sandbox with timeout and resource limits |
| GET | `/sandboxes` | List with filtering and pagination |
| GET | `/sandboxes/{sandboxId}` | Retrieve full details |
| DELETE | `/sandboxes/{sandboxId}` | Remove sandbox |
| POST | `/sandboxes/{sandboxId}/pause` | Pause execution (async) |
| POST | `/sandboxes/{sandboxId}/resume` | Resume paused sandbox |
| POST | `/sandboxes/{sandboxId}/renew-expiration` | Extend TTL |
| GET | `/sandboxes/{sandboxId}/endpoints/{port}` | Access service endpoint |

### Lifecycle States

Supported transitions: Pending → Running → Pausing → Paused → Stopping → Terminated, plus Failed state for error handling.

### Configuration Options

- CPU/memory/GPU resource limits (Kubernetes-style: "500m", "512Mi")
- Required entrypoint specification
- Environment variables
- Private registry authentication
- Opaque extensions field

## Code Execution API (execd)

**Authentication:** `X-EXECD-ACCESS-TOKEN` header required

### Health & Context Management

- `GET /ping` – Service availability check
- `GET /code/contexts` – List active contexts by language
- `POST /code/context` – Create execution context
- `DELETE /code/contexts/{context_id}` – Remove specific context

### Code & Command Execution

- `POST /code` – Execute code with streaming output
- `DELETE /code` – Interrupt execution
- `POST /command` – Shell command execution
- `GET /command/status/{session}` – Check command status
- `GET /command/output/{session}` – Retrieve accumulated output

### File Operations

- `GET /files/info` – Metadata retrieval
- `POST /files/upload` – Multipart file uploads
- `GET /files/download` – Download with range support
- `DELETE /files` – Remove files
- `POST /files/mv` – Move/rename operations
- `GET /files/search` – Glob pattern searching
- `POST /files/replace` – Batch content replacement
- `POST /files/permissions` – Unix-style permission changes

### Directory Management

- `POST /directories` – Create with mkdir -p semantics
- `DELETE /directories` – Recursive deletion

### System Monitoring

- `GET /metrics` – Current resource usage
- `GET /metrics/watch` – Real-time SSE stream

## Technical Features

**Streaming:** Server-Sent Events with event types: init, status, stdout, stderr, result, execution_complete, execution_count, error

**Resources:** Flexible limits mirroring Kubernetes format (cpu, memory, gpu)

**Permissions:** Owner, group, and octal mode (e.g., 755) support

# OpenSandbox Server - README Summary

## Overview
OpenSandbox Server is a "production-grade, FastAPI-based service for managing the lifecycle of containerized sandboxes." It functions as a control plane for creating, running, monitoring, and disposing of isolated execution environments.

## Core Features

**Lifecycle APIs**: REST interfaces supporting create, start, pause, resume, and delete operations.

**Pluggable Runtimes**:
- Docker (production-ready)
- Kubernetes (production-ready with operator deployment)

**Key Capabilities**:
- Automatic expiration with configurable TTL and renewal
- API Key authentication via `OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY` header
- Networking modes: host (shared network) and bridge (isolated with HTTP routing)
- Resource quotas using CPU/memory limits
- Registry support for public and private images

## Requirements

- Python 3.10+
- Docker Engine 20.10+ OR Kubernetes 1.21.1+
- Package manager: uv (recommended) or pip
- Linux, macOS, or Windows with WSL2

## Installation & Quick Start

```bash
uv pip install opensandbox-server
opensandbox-server init-config ~/.sandbox.toml --example docker
opensandbox-server
```

Health check: `curl http://localhost:8080/health`

## Configuration (TOML)

**Server Section**:
- `host`: Bind interface (default: "0.0.0.0")
- `port`: Listen port (default: 8080)
- `log_level`: Python logging level (default: "INFO")
- `api_key`: Authentication key (null = disabled for dev)
- `eip`: Public IP for endpoint resolution

**Runtime Section**:
- `type`: "docker" or "kubernetes"
- `execd_image`: execd container image URI

**Docker Configuration**:
- `network_mode`: "host" or "bridge"
- `host_ip`: Reachable host for bridge-mode endpoints
- `drop_capabilities`: Security hardening list
- `no_new_privileges`: Boolean flag
- `pids_limit`: Fork bomb protection

**Kubernetes Configuration**:
- `kubeconfig_path`: Path to kubeconfig
- `namespace`: Sandbox namespace
- `workload_provider`: "batchsandbox" or "agent-sandbox"
- `informer_enabled`: Watch-based cache (beta)

**Egress Configuration** (for network policies):
- `image`: Egress sidecar image (required when using networkPolicy)

## API Documentation

Interactive docs available at:
- Swagger UI: `http://localhost:8080/docs`
- ReDoc: `http://localhost:8080/redoc`

**Authentication**: All endpoints (except `/health`, `/docs`, `/redoc`) require the `OPEN-SANDBOX-API-KEY` header when enabled.

**Example Endpoints**:
- `POST /v1/sandboxes` - Create sandbox
- `GET /v1/sandboxes/{id}` - Get details
- `GET /v1/sandboxes/{id}/endpoints/{port}` - Resolve endpoint
- `POST /v1/sandboxes/{id}/renew-expiration` - Extend TTL
- `DELETE /v1/sandboxes/{id}` - Delete sandbox

## Sandbox Lifecycle States

States include: Pending → Running (or Paused) → Stopping → Terminated/Failed

## Architecture

**Components**:
- API Layer: HTTP handling and validation
- Service Layer: Business logic
- Middleware: Authentication, logging
- Configuration: Centralized TOML management
- Runtime Implementations: Platform-specific orchestration

## Security Features

Supports capability dropping, privilege escalation prevention, AppArmor profiles, fork bomb limits, and optional seccomp enforcement for Docker containers.

# OpenSandbox Ingress Gateway Overview

## Core Functionality

The OpenSandbox Ingress component is "an HTTP/WebSocket reverse proxy that routes to sandbox instances." It monitors sandbox custom resources (either BatchSandbox or AgentSandbox types) within a Kubernetes namespace and forwards incoming requests to the appropriate sandbox endpoints.

## Configuration Options

Launch the service using command-line arguments:

```bash
go run main.go \
  --namespace <target-namespace> \
  --provider-type <batchsandbox|agent-sandbox> \
  --mode <header|uri> \
  --port 28888 \
  --log-level info
```

Key settings include the target Kubernetes namespace, sandbox provider type selection, routing mode preference, listening port, and logging verbosity.

## Two Routing Strategies

**Header Mode (default):** Extracts routing information from either the `OpenSandbox-Ingress-To` header or the `Host` header using the format `<sandbox-id>-<port>`. This approach works when headers can be customized.

**URI Mode:** Embeds routing data directly in the URL path as `/<sandbox-id>/<sandbox-port>/<path-to-request>`. This method suits scenarios where header modification isn't feasible.

## Request Handling

The ingress resolves sandbox endpoints differently based on provider type: BatchSandbox instances expose endpoints via annotations, while AgentSandbox resources use the `status.serviceFQDN` field. Request paths are preserved during forwarding, with responses mapped according to HTTP status codes indicating success, client errors (404), service unavailability (503), or gateway issues (502).

# OpenSandbox Egress Sidecar Component

## Core Functionality

The Egress Sidecar provides "FQDN-based egress control" by running alongside sandbox application containers to enforce network policies. It operates in the shared network namespace, intercepting and filtering outbound traffic based on domain names and IP addresses.

## How It Manages Network Policies Per Sandbox

The component implements a two-layer enforcement model:

**Layer 1 - DNS Proxy:** Runs on `127.0.0.1:15353` with iptables redirecting all port 53 traffic. The proxy filters DNS queries against the allowlist, returning `NXDOMAIN` for denied domains. This prevents applications from resolving prohibited hosts.

**Layer 2 - Network Filter (dns+nft mode):** Uses nftables to enforce IP-level rules. "Resolved IPs for allowed domains are added to dynamic allow sets with TTL" so the system maintains default-deny posture while permitting resolved addresses.

Each sandbox gets its own policy instance via the HTTP API, supporting both allowlist (default deny) and blocklist (default allow) approaches.

## Configuration Options

**Policy Management:**
- Bootstrap policies via `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_RULES` environment variable (JSON format)
- Runtime updates through `POST /policy` endpoint
- Default is deny-all; empty bodies reset to this state

**Operational Settings:**
- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MODE`: `dns` (proxy only) or `dns+nft` (with network filtering)
- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_HTTP_ADDR`: Server listen address (default `:18080`)
- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_TOKEN`: Optional authentication header requirement
- `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_MAX_NS`: Cap on whitelisted nameservers (default `3`)
- DoH/DoT blocking controls via `OPENSANDBOX_EGRESS_BLOCK_DOH_443` and blocklists

**Requirements:**
- Linux kernel with iptables support
- `CAP_NET_ADMIN` capability for the sidecar only (application containers run unprivileged)

# execd: OpenSandbox Execution Daemon

## Overview
execd is a Go-based HTTP API service that manages code execution, command handling, and file operations within sandbox containers. Built on the Beego framework, it translates external requests into runtime actions.

## Implementation Language
**Go 1.24+** – The daemon is written in Go and compiled as a standalone binary with minimal dependencies.

## Core Architecture

### How It Works
execd functions as a dispatcher that routes requests to appropriate backends:

1. **Jupyter Integration** – Maintains long-lived kernel sessions via WebSocket connections for stateful code execution
2. **Shell Executor** – Handles synchronous and background commands with process group management
3. **Filesystem Layer** – Provides CRUD operations with chunked upload/download support

The system translates HTTP requests into actions handled by `pkg/runtime`, which abstracts away backend differences.

## Supported Languages

**Jupyter-based execution:**
- Python (IPython kernel)
- Java (IJava)
- JavaScript (IJavaScript)
- TypeScript (ITypeScript)
- Go (gophernotes)
- Bash

**Native executors:**
- Shell commands (synchronous and background)

## API Endpoints

Key operations include:

- **Code Execution** – `POST /code` accepts language and code payload, streams results via Server-Sent Events
- **Commands** – `POST /command` for shell execution with stdout/stderr streaming
- **File Operations** – CRUD helpers supporting glob-based search and chunked transfers
- **Monitoring** – `/metrics` endpoint exposes CPU, memory, and uptime data
- **Health** – `/ping` for service verification

## Code Execution Flow

1. Client sends POST request with language specification and source code
2. execd detects language and routes to appropriate Jupyter kernel
3. Code executes in isolated kernel session maintaining state
4. Results stream back as SSE events (stdout, stderr, execution status)
5. Graceful shutdown window allows clients to drain final output

## Command Execution

The system supports:
- **Foreground commands** – Synchronous execution with real-time output streaming
- **Background commands** – Detached processes returning immediately
- **Signal forwarding** – Proper handling via process groups for clean interruption

## File Operations

- Create, read, update, delete files within sandbox
- Glob-based file search and filtering
- Chunked upload/download with resume capability
- Permission management

## Performance Characteristics

- Typical latency: 50-200ms for code execution, <5ms for file metadata
- Idle resource usage: ~50MB memory, <1% CPU

- `/e2e` — Playwright end-to-end tests
- `/examples` — Exported conversation examples (static HTML)

### 2. **Docker & Container Setup**

**docker-compose.yml architecture:**
- **bifrost** service — Anthropic LLM gateway (maximhq/bifrost:latest)
  - Manages API keys centrally
  - Routes LLM requests to Anthropic API

- **app** service — FastAPI backend (built from backend/Dockerfile)
  - Hosts frontend static files
  - Runs MCP SSE server at `/mcp`

  - Built from sidecar/Dockerfile
  - Spawned on-demand per session via Docker SDK
  - Runs Claude Agent SDK in Node.js
  - Port: 3000

**Network:**
- All containers connect via `agent-sandbox` Docker bridge network
- gVisor runtime (`runsc`) provides sandboxing for sidecar containers

### 3. **Sidecar Architecture** (`/sidecar`)

**Key files:**
- `src/server.ts` — Express.js server running Claude Agent SDK
  - Receives `/query` POST requests from backend with message + system prompt
  - Streams responses via SSE (Server-Sent Events)
  - Runs Claude CLI subprocess with SDK isolation
  - Langfuse tracing support (optional)
  - Skill allowlist enforcement (denies unknown local skills)
  - Pre-flight reachability checks for MCP and LLM endpoints
  - SDK idle timeout: 600s (configurable via `SDK_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS`)

**Docker setup:**
- Multi-stage build: Node.js + Python base image
- TypeScript compiled to `dist/` at build time
- Skills mounted read-only at `/app/.claude/skills/`
- Plugins mounted read-only at `/app/plugins/`
- tmpfs at `~/.claude` for temporary session data

### 4. **Backend Architecture** (`/backend`)

**Core components:**

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `app/main.py` | FastAPI app, routes, middleware, lifespan management |
| `app/agent.py` | System prompt building, orchestrator agent definition, streaming logic |
| `app/config.py` | Configuration loading from env vars (models, container limits, API URLs) |
| `app/session_manager.py` | Per-session DuckDB instance lifecycle management |
| `app/database.py` | DuckDB wrapper (execute_query, load_csv/json/parquet/xlsx) |
| `app/container_manager.py` | Docker SDK for spawning/managing gVisor sidecar containers |
| `app/mcp_sse.py` | MCP server implementation (tools: execute_sql, render_chart, ask_user_question, create_skill, save_memory, recall_memories, forget_memory) |
| `app/memory_store.py` | SQLite-backed memory persistence (`data/memory.db`) |
| `app/agent_memory.py` | Loading/saving memories to disk (`data/memories/{user_id}/MEMORY.md`) |
| `app/pending_questions.py` | Stores pending user questions from agent (used for interactive clarification) |
| `app/proxy.py` | HTTP proxy to Bifrost gateway (rewrites model names per config) |
| `app/skills.py` | Skill file creation & validation |
| `app/tracing.py` | Langfuse integration |

**Routes:**
- `/api/chat` — Main chat endpoint (POST, streams SSE)
- `/api/chat/edit` — Edit message and restart conversation
- `/api/chat/respond` — Respond to agent's pending questions
- `/api/tables` — List/upload tables, drop tables
- `/api/query` — Direct SQL query execution (editor mode)
- `/api/conversations` — Create/load/delete/rename conversations
- `/api/skills` — List/create/enable/disable/delete skills
- `/api/memories` — List/delete memories
- `/api/config` — Fetch frontend configuration
- `/api/session` — Session lifecycle (create, check, close)
- `/api/langfuse-status` — Check if Langfuse is enabled
- `/mcp/messages/` — MCP SSE transport endpoint

**Session management:**
- Per-session DuckDB file: `/tmp/duckdb-data-agent-{session_id}.duckdb`
- Session lifecycle: last-access based (5 min idle TTL by default)
- Conversation history stored in `data/conversations/` SQLite DB (scoped by session)
- Frontend generates `X-Session-ID` header (UUID v4)

### 5. **Frontend Architecture** (`/frontend`)

**Key components:**

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `src/App.tsx` | Root component, layout management |
| `src/components/AgentPanel.tsx` | Chat interface, message rendering |
| `src/components/MessageBubble.tsx` | Individual message rendering (text, inline queries, charts) |
| `src/components/ChartWidget.tsx` | Plotly chart renderer |
| `src/components/VegaLiteChartWidget.tsx` | Vega-Lite chart renderer |
| `src/components/QueryEditor.tsx` | SQL editor for direct queries |
| `src/components/Sidebar.tsx` | Tables list, conversation history, skills, memories |
| `src/components/FileUpload.tsx` | Drag-drop file upload |
| `src/contexts/AgentContext.tsx` | Chat message state, streaming management |
| `src/contexts/ConversationContext.tsx` | Conversation list, history persistence |
| `src/contexts/SessionContext.tsx` | Session ID, DuckDB session state |
| `src/hooks/useAgent.ts` | Hook for chat operations, message editing/deletion |
| `src/agent/agentService.ts` | SSE client parsing, message/chart/tool-result extraction |

**Key features:**
- Real-time token streaming via SSE
- Live cross-conversation streaming (multiple chats run concurrently)
- Interactive clarification (agent asks user questions via modal)
- Chart library toggle (Plotly ↔ Vega-Lite, persisted to localStorage)
- Dark/light theme toggle
- I18n (English/Traditional Chinese)
- Message edit/delete with conversation rewind
- Conversation history sidebar
- Skill library with slash command autocomplete
- Memory browser
- Export as self-contained HTML

**SSE message types:**
- `text` — Agent response text
- `tool_call` — Agent called a tool
- `tool_result` — Tool execution result (includes chart_spec, dashboard_html)
- `thinking` — Agent's intermediate reasoning
- `pending_question` — Agent asking user for clarification
- `answer_done` — Turn complete (includes duration_ms)

### 6. **Container Isolation & Deployment**

**Container per session:**
- Backend spawns a new sidecar container per session using Docker SDK
- Container spec:
  - Image: `duckdb-agent-sidecar:latest`
  - Runtime: `runsc` (gVisor for security sandboxing)
  - Memory: 256–512 MB (configurable)
  - CPU: 0.5–1 core (configurable)
  - Network: `agent-sandbox` bridge (isolated from host)
  - Read-only root filesystem
  - All capabilities dropped
  - No host filesystem access
  - Volume mounts:
    - Skills: `/app/.claude/skills/` (read-only)
    - Plugins: `/app/plugins/` (read-only)

**Lifecycle:**
- Created on first request (lazy initialization)
- Garbage collected on idle timeout (300s default) or max lifetime (3600s)
- gVisor DNS workaround: containers resolve Docker hostnames via `/etc/hosts` (built by backend)

**No Kubernetes manifests** — Project is single-server Docker Compose based.

### 7. **Agent Mode vs. Agent Mode (Container vs. Local)**

The project has **two execution modes**:

**Container Mode (Default):**
- Backend spawns a sidecar container per session
- Sidecar runs Claude Agent SDK (TypeScript) in Node.js
- Backend communicates via HTTP `/query` endpoint
- Provides process isolation, sandboxing, multi-tenant safety
- Used in docker-compose deployment

**Agent Mode (Local subprocess):**
- Backend runs Claude Agent SDK directly (Python SDK)
- Agent code runs in backend process
- Used in `make dev` or native development
- No container overhead, but less isolation

Code switches modes based on `ContainerManager` availability. The backend checks if Docker is reachable; if yes, container mode is used.

### 8. **Recent Docs & Plans**

**Current focus (Feb 26 - Mar 3):**
- `/docs/plans/2026-03-03-inline-dashboard-rendering.md` — Implement `render_dashboard` MCP tool for `/data:build-dashboard` command
  - Adds new HtmlDashboardWidget React component
  - Captures HTML in SSE pipeline (like render_chart)
  - Renders in sandboxed `<iframe srcdoc>` 
  - Supports expand fullscreen, download, open in new tab

**Completed features (tracked in docs):**
- FastAPI Agent SDK integration
- Multi-format file upload (CSV, JSON, Parquet, Excel)
- Per-user DuckDB sessions with persistence
- Containerized runtime with gVisor
- Bifrost LLM gateway for credential management
- Subagent routing (sql-analyst for queries)
- Live cross-conversation streaming
- Skill creation & discovery
- Agent memory system
- Chart library switching (Plotly ↔ Vega-Lite)
- E2E tests with Playwright
- Interactive clarification (ask_user_question)

### 9. **Key Configuration (via .env)**

```python
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY              # Bifrost reads this
BIFROST_BASE_URL              # http://bifrost:8080 (docker-compose)
BACKEND_BASE_URL              # http://duckdb-data-agent:10000
ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL            # claude-sonnet-4-6 (default)
SQL_SUBAGENT_MODEL            # inherit or specific model
MAX_TOTAL_SIZE_BYTES          # 500 MB (default)
CONTAINER_IMAGE               # duckdb-agent-sidecar:latest
CONTAINER_RUNTIME             # runc or runsc (gVisor)
CONTAINER_MEMORY_LIMIT        # 256m-512m
CONTAINER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS # 900
LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY           # Optional tracing
LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY           # Optional tracing
```

### 10. **How the System Currently Works**

**Request flow:**
1. User types message in React frontend, frontend generates `X-Session-ID` (UUID)
2. Frontend POSTs to `/api/chat` with message, session_id, conversation_history
3. Backend gets/creates DuckDB session, spawns sidecar container if needed
4. Backend POSTs `/query` to sidecar with system prompt, conversation history
5. Sidecar runs Claude Agent SDK (spawns CLI subprocess)
6. Agent makes tool calls: `execute_sql`, `render_chart`, `ask_user_question`, etc.
7. Sidecar's MCP handler calls backend's MCP SSE endpoint at `/mcp/messages/`
8. Backend's MCP server executes tools (SQL queries, renders charts) and returns results
9. SDK streams response as SSE events (`text`, `tool_call`, `tool_result`, `thinking`, etc.)
10. Frontend parses SSE, renders text/charts/tables inline, displays in chat

**Key insight:** The backend manages agent lifecycle but **doesn't execute the agent code itself**. The sidecar container is the actual execution environment. This allows:
- Strong process isolation
- Per-session resource limits
- Multi-tenancy support
- Easy horizontal scaling (spawn containers on demand)

---

**Files of interest for future development:**
- `/backend/app/agent.py` (150+ lines) — System prompt, orchestrator setup
- `/sidecar/src/server.ts` (400+ lines) — Agent SDK runner, stream handling
- `/docs/plans/2026-03-03-inline-dashboard-rendering.md` — Next major feature (dashboard rendering)
- `/backend/app/mcp_sse.py` (400+ lines) — Tool definitions and execution

# OpenSandbox Kubernetes Controller: Deployment Resources

## Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)

The project defines two primary CRDs:

1. **BatchSandbox** - Manages creation of multiple sandbox instances with specifications for replicas, templates, and optional task scheduling
2. **Pool** - Maintains pre-warmed resource pools with configurable buffer sizes and capacity limits

## Sandbox Management Architecture

The controller implements a Kubernetes operator pattern with the following characteristics:

- **Automated lifecycle management** through custom resources
- **Resource pooling** enabling rapid sandbox provisioning by pre-warming container resources
- **Optional task orchestration** for executing custom workloads within sandboxes

Multi-language client libraries providing high-level abstractions:
- Python (production-ready, published as `opensandbox` on PyPI)

**execd Daemon** is the most critical internal component. It runs inside every sandbox container and provides:

- File operations (CRUD, glob search, chunked upload/download, permission management)
- System metrics (CPU, memory, uptime)

- **Option 1 (Replace ContainerManager)**: OpenSandbox replaces your custom Docker SDK code, but the deployment target stays Docker only. You'd use OpenSandbox's Docker runtime instead of calling Docker SDK directly. No Kubernetes support.

- **Option 3 (Replace + add K8s)**: Same replacement of the custom Docker code, BUT also adds Kubernetes as a deployment option. Users could choose:
  - `docker-compose` with OpenSandbox's Docker runtime (like today, but managed by OpenSandbox)

Now let me propose approaches. Here are **3 approaches** with trade-offs:

---

### Approach A: Thin Adapter (Recommended)

Replace `ContainerManager` with a new `SandboxManager` that wraps the OpenSandbox Python SDK. The backend calls OpenSandbox's HTTP API for lifecycle, but still communicates with the sidecar via the existing `/query` HTTP endpoint.

**How it works:**
1. OpenSandbox server manages container creation/destruction/timeout
2. Backend uses `opensandbox` Python SDK to create sandboxes with the custom sidecar image
3. After sandbox creation, backend still POSTs to the sidecar's `/query` endpoint directly (resolved via OpenSandbox's endpoint API)
4. Config toggle selects Docker vs K8s runtime

**Pros:** Minimal changes to backend/sidecar logic. Clean separation. Leverages OpenSandbox for what it's good at (lifecycle) without rearchitecting the agent communication path.

**Cons:** Two HTTP hops for lifecycle (backend → OpenSandbox → Docker/K8s), but this is only at sandbox creation time, not per-query.

---

### Approach B: Full OpenSandbox Integration

Use OpenSandbox's execd for both lifecycle AND command execution. Replace the sidecar's Express server with execd, and run the Claude Agent SDK as a long-running command inside the sandbox.

**How it works:**
1. OpenSandbox creates sandboxes with a base Node.js image + execd injected
2. Backend uses execd's command API to start the Agent SDK server
3. Backend communicates with the agent via execd's streaming command API

**Pros:** Fully aligned with OpenSandbox's architecture. No custom sidecar image needed.

**Cons:** Major rearchitecture of the sidecar. Adds latency (execd as intermediary). Loses fine-grained control over the Agent SDK server. Higher risk.

---

### Approach C: Dual Runtime (Legacy + OpenSandbox)

Keep the existing `ContainerManager` for Docker and add OpenSandbox only for K8s.

**How it works:**
1. Docker deployment: uses existing `ContainerManager` (unchanged)
2. K8s deployment: uses OpenSandbox with agent-sandbox provider
3. Config selects which runtime to use

**Pros:** Zero risk to existing Docker workflow. K8s support added independently.

**Cons:** Two codepaths to maintain. Inconsistent behavior between Docker and K8s deployments. Duplicated lifecycle logic.

---

**My recommendation: Approach A (Thin Adapter).** It gives you both Docker and K8s support through a single codepath, minimizes changes to existing agent communication, and leverages OpenSandbox for what it does best — container lifecycle management. The existing `/query` endpoint on the sidecar remains the communication channel, so the agent logic is untouched.

    42→        # On macOS, Docker containers are in a VM and their bridge IPs are
    43→        # not routable from the host, so we must go via the published port.
    44→        # When the backend itself runs inside a container (docker-compose) or
    45→        # on Linux, both containers share the same network and the direct
    46→        # container IP is reachable — 127.0.0.1 would point at the backend
    47→        # container itself, not the host.
    48→        _on_macos_host = sys.platform == "darwin" and not os.path.exists("/.dockerenv")
    49→        if self.host_port and _on_macos_host:
    50→            return f"http://127.0.0.1:{self.host_port}"
    51→        return f"http://{self.ip_address}:{self.port}"
    52→
    53→
    54→class ContainerManager:
    55→    """Manages per-session gVisor-sandboxed sidecar containers."""
    56→
    57→    def __init__(self, config: ContainerConfig | None = None):
    58→        self._config = config or ContainerConfig()
    59→        self._client = docker.from_env()
    60→        self._containers: dict[str, ContainerInfo] = {}
    61→
    62→    def _resolve_network_hosts(self) -> dict[str, str]:
    63→        """Resolve container hostnames to IPs on the sidecar network.
    64→
    65→        gVisor's netstack doesn't use Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11),
    66→        so DNS resolution fails inside runsc containers. We build an
    67→        extra_hosts mapping from container names to their IPs on the
    68→        shared network so /etc/hosts provides the resolution instead.
    69→        """

    72→            network = self._client.networks.get(self._config.network)
    73→            network.reload()
    74→            containers = network.attrs.get("Containers", {})
    75→            for _cid, info in containers.items():
    76→                name = info.get("Name", "")
    77→                ipv4 = info.get("IPv4Address", "")

    93→        address that containers on that network can actually route to.

    97→            network.reload()

    99→                gateway = cfg.get("Gateway")

   147→        # Strategy depends on platform and runtime:

   270→        lifetime_cutoff = now - timedelta(seconds=self._config.max_lifetime_seconds)
   271→        expired = [
   272→            sid for sid, info in self._containers.items()
   273→            if info.last_activity < idle_cutoff or info.created_at < lifetime_cutoff

   341→        CONTAINER_IMAGE,
   342→        CONTAINER_RUNTIME,
   343→        CONTAINER_MEMORY_LIMIT,
   344→        CONTAINER_CPU_LIMIT,
   345→        CONTAINER_MAX_LIFETIME_SECONDS,
   346→        CONTAINER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
   347→        CONTAINER_NETWORK,
   348→    )

   353→            runtime=CONTAINER_RUNTIME,

import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import docker

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


@dataclass
class ContainerConfig:
    image: str = "duckdb-agent-sidecar:latest"
    runtime: str = "runsc"
    memory_limit: str = "256m"
    cpu_limit: float = 0.5
    max_lifetime_seconds: int = 3600
    idle_timeout_seconds: int = 300
    network: str = "agent-sandbox"


@dataclass
class ContainerInfo:
    container_id: str
    session_id: str
    ip_address: str
    port: int = 3000
    created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    last_activity: datetime = field(default=None)
    _container: object = field(default=None, repr=False)

    host_port: int | None = None

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.last_activity is None:
            self.last_activity = self.created_at

    @property
    def url(self) -> str:
        # Use the published host port only when running natively on macOS.
        # On macOS, Docker containers are in a VM and their bridge IPs are
        # not routable from the host, so we must go via the published port.
        # When the backend itself runs inside a container (docker-compose) or
        # on Linux, both containers share the same network and the direct
        # container IP is reachable — 127.0.0.1 would point at the backend
        # container itself, not the host.
        _on_macos_host = sys.platform == "darwin" and not os.path.exists("/.dockerenv")
        if self.host_port and _on_macos_host:
            return f"http://127.0.0.1:{self.host_port}"
        return f"http://{self.ip_address}:{self.port}"


class ContainerManager:
    """Manages per-session gVisor-sandboxed sidecar containers."""

    def __init__(self, config: ContainerConfig | None = None):
        self._config = config or ContainerConfig()
        self._client = docker.from_env()
        self._containers: dict[str, ContainerInfo] = {}

    def _resolve_network_hosts(self) -> dict[str, str]:
        """Resolve container hostnames to IPs on the sidecar network.

        gVisor's netstack doesn't use Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11),
        so DNS resolution fails inside runsc containers. We build an
        extra_hosts mapping from container names to their IPs on the
        shared network so /etc/hosts provides the resolution instead.
        """
        hosts: dict[str, str] = {}
        try:
            network = self._client.networks.get(self._config.network)
            network.reload()
            containers = network.attrs.get("Containers", {})
            for _cid, info in containers.items():
                name = info.get("Name", "")
                ipv4 = info.get("IPv4Address", "")
                if name and ipv4:
                    # Strip CIDR suffix (e.g. "172.20.0.2/16" -> "172.20.0.2")
                    ip = ipv4.split("/")[0]
                    hosts[name] = ip
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning("Failed to resolve network hosts: %s", e)
        return hosts

    def _resolve_host_gateway_ip(self) -> str | None:
        """Get the host IP reachable from sidecar containers.

        Docker's "host-gateway" magic value resolves to the docker0 bridge IP,
        not to the gateway of our custom network. Under gVisor the value may
        also not be honoured at all. Instead we read the gateway IP directly
        from the sidecar network's IPAM config — this is the host-side bridge
        address that containers on that network can actually route to.
        """
        try:
            network = self._client.networks.get(self._config.network)
            network.reload()
            for cfg in network.attrs.get("IPAM", {}).get("Config", []):
                gateway = cfg.get("Gateway")
                if gateway:
                    logger.info("Resolved host.docker.internal gateway to %s", gateway)
                    return gateway
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning("Failed to resolve host gateway IP: %s", e)
        return None

    def create(self, session_id: str, env: dict[str, str]) -> ContainerInfo:
        """Spin up a new sidecar container for a session."""
        if session_id in self._containers:
            return self._containers[session_id]

        # Skills volume: mount the host skills directory into the sidecar
        # so it can discover dynamically created skills.
        skills_host_path = os.environ.get("SKILLS_HOST_PATH", "")
        if not skills_host_path:
            # When running natively on the host (not inside Docker),
            # compute the skills directory from this file's location.
            # container_manager.py is at backend/app/, skills/ is at project root.
            if not os.path.exists("/.dockerenv"):
                fallback = os.path.abspath(
                    os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "..", "skills")
                )
                if os.path.isdir(fallback):
                    skills_host_path = fallback
        # Plugins volume: mount the host plugins directory into the sidecar
        # so the SDK can discover locally installed plugins.
        plugins_host_path = os.environ.get("PLUGINS_HOST_PATH", "")
        if not plugins_host_path:
            if not os.path.exists("/.dockerenv"):
                fallback_plugins = os.path.abspath(
                    os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "..", "plugins")
                )
                if os.path.isdir(fallback_plugins):
                    plugins_host_path = fallback_plugins

        volumes = {}
        if skills_host_path:
            abs_skills_path = os.path.abspath(skills_host_path)
            volumes[abs_skills_path] = {"bind": "/app/.claude/skills", "mode": "ro"}
        if plugins_host_path:
            abs_plugins_path = os.path.abspath(plugins_host_path)
            volumes[abs_plugins_path] = {"bind": "/app/plugins", "mode": "ro"}

        # Resolve container hostnames to IPs for gVisor DNS compatibility
        extra_hosts = self._resolve_network_hosts()
        # Resolve host.docker.internal so the sidecar can reach the host.
        # Strategy depends on platform and runtime:
        #
        # - macOS Docker Desktop (any runtime): "host-gateway" works correctly
        #   and resolves to the Mac host.  The IPAM gateway IP points to the
        #   bridge gateway *inside* the Linux VM, which is NOT the Mac host,
        #   so we must NOT use it here.
        #
        # - Linux + runc: "host-gateway" resolves to the docker0 bridge IP
        #   which is routable from the container.
        #
        # - Linux + runsc (gVisor): "host-gateway" may not be honoured.
        #   Read the actual gateway IP from the network's IPAM config instead.
        _on_macos_host = sys.platform == "darwin" and not os.path.exists("/.dockerenv")
        _using_gvisor = self._config.runtime == "runsc"

        if _using_gvisor and not _on_macos_host:
            host_gateway_ip = self._resolve_host_gateway_ip()
            if host_gateway_ip:
                extra_hosts["host.docker.internal"] = host_gateway_ip
            else:
                extra_hosts["host.docker.internal"] = "host-gateway"
                logger.warning(
                    "Could not resolve host gateway IP from IPAM; falling back to "
                    "host-gateway magic value (may not work under gVisor on Linux)"
                )
        else:
            extra_hosts["host.docker.internal"] = "host-gateway"
        if extra_hosts:
            logger.info("Sidecar extra_hosts: %s", extra_hosts)

        container = self._client.containers.run(
            image=self._config.image,
            detach=True,
            runtime=self._config.runtime,
            mem_limit=self._config.memory_limit,
            nano_cpus=int(self._config.cpu_limit * 1e9),
            read_only=True,
            cap_drop=["ALL"],
            security_opt=["no-new-privileges"],
            tmpfs={
                "/tmp": "size=50m",
                "/home/appuser": "size=50m,uid=1000,gid=1000",
                # Separate tmpfs for .claude so it stays owned by appuser
                # and writable for CLI session data, debug logs, etc.
                "/home/appuser/.claude": "size=10m,uid=1000,gid=1000",
            },
            **({"volumes": volumes} if volumes else {}),
            network=self._config.network,
            environment=env,
            extra_hosts=extra_hosts or None,
            # Use public DNS so gVisor's netstack can resolve external hosts
            # (Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 doesn't work under runsc)
            dns=["8.8.8.8", "8.8.4.4"],
            # Publish port to a random host port so the host-side backend
            # can reach the sidecar (macOS cannot route to bridge IPs)
            ports={"3000/tcp": None},
            labels={
                "app": "duckdb-agent-sidecar",
                "session_id": session_id,
            },
            auto_remove=False,
        )

        container.reload()
        networks = container.attrs.get("NetworkSettings", {}).get("Networks", {})
        network_info = networks.get(self._config.network, {})
        ip_address = network_info.get("IPAddress", "127.0.0.1")

        # Extract the dynamically assigned host port
        port_bindings = container.attrs.get("NetworkSettings", {}).get("Ports", {})
        host_port = None
        tcp_bindings = port_bindings.get("3000/tcp")
        if tcp_bindings and len(tcp_bindings) > 0:
            host_port = int(tcp_bindings[0].get("HostPort", 0)) or None

        info = ContainerInfo(
            container_id=container.id,
            session_id=session_id,
            ip_address=ip_address,
            host_port=host_port,
            _container=container,
        )
        self._containers[session_id] = info
        logger.info(
            "Created sidecar container %s for session %s at %s",
            container.id[:12],
            session_id,
            info.url,
        )
        return info

    def get(self, session_id: str) -> ContainerInfo | None:
        """Get container info for a session."""
        return self._containers.get(session_id)

    def touch(self, session_id: str) -> None:
        """Update last_activity timestamp for a session's container."""
        info = self._containers.get(session_id)
        if info is not None:
            info.last_activity = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    def stop(self, session_id: str) -> None:
        """Stop and remove the container for a session."""
        info = self._containers.pop(session_id, None)
        if info is None:
            return

        container = info._container
        try:
            container.stop(timeout=5)
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning("Failed to stop container %s: %s", info.container_id[:12], e)
        try:
            container.remove(force=True)
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning("Failed to remove container %s: %s", info.container_id[:12], e)

        logger.info("Stopped sidecar container %s for session %s", info.container_id[:12], session_id)

    def cleanup_expired(self) -> int:
        """Remove containers that are idle or have exceeded max lifetime."""
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        idle_cutoff = now - timedelta(seconds=self._config.idle_timeout_seconds)
        lifetime_cutoff = now - timedelta(seconds=self._config.max_lifetime_seconds)
        expired = [
            sid for sid, info in self._containers.items()
            if info.last_activity < idle_cutoff or info.created_at < lifetime_cutoff
        ]
        for sid in expired:
            logger.info("Container for session %s expired (idle or max lifetime), removing", sid)
            self.stop(sid)
        return len(expired)

    def shutdown_all(self) -> None:
        """Stop and remove all sidecar containers. Called on backend shutdown.

        In addition to the in-memory registry, queries Docker for any
        containers with the ``app=duckdb-agent-sidecar`` label so that
        orphaned containers (from a previous crash, SIGKILL, or race
        during creation) are also cleaned up.
        """
        # 1. Snapshot tracked IDs before stopping (stop() pops from the dict).
        tracked_ids = {info.container_id for info in self._containers.values()}
        session_ids = list(self._containers.keys())
        for sid in session_ids:
            self.stop(sid)
        tracked_count = len(session_ids)

        # 2. Find any remaining sidecar containers via Docker labels.
        orphan_count = self._cleanup_by_label(exclude_ids=tracked_ids)

        logger.info(
            "Shut down %d tracked + %d orphaned sidecar containers",
            tracked_count,
            orphan_count,
        )

    def _cleanup_by_label(self, *, exclude_ids: set[str] | None = None) -> int:
        """Stop and remove all Docker containers with the sidecar label.

        Args:
            exclude_ids: Container IDs to skip (already handled elsewhere).

        Returns the number of containers cleaned up.
        """
        skip = exclude_ids or set()
        cleaned = 0
        try:
            containers = self._client.containers.list(
                filters={"label": "app=duckdb-agent-sidecar"},
                all=True,
            )
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning("Failed to list sidecar containers by label: %s", e)
            return 0

        for container in containers:
            if container.id in skip:
                continue  # already handled
            try:
                container.stop(timeout=5)
            except Exception as e:
                logger.warning("Failed to stop orphaned container %s: %s", container.id[:12], e)
            try:
                container.remove(force=True)
            except Exception as e:
                logger.warning("Failed to remove orphaned container %s: %s", container.id[:12], e)
            logger.info("Cleaned up orphaned sidecar container %s", container.id[:12])
            cleaned += 1
        return cleaned


try:
    from app.config import (
        CONTAINER_IMAGE,
        CONTAINER_RUNTIME,
        CONTAINER_MEMORY_LIMIT,
        CONTAINER_CPU_LIMIT,
        CONTAINER_MAX_LIFETIME_SECONDS,
        CONTAINER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
        CONTAINER_NETWORK,
    )

    container_manager = ContainerManager(
        ContainerConfig(
            image=CONTAINER_IMAGE,
            runtime=CONTAINER_RUNTIME,
            memory_limit=CONTAINER_MEMORY_LIMIT,
            cpu_limit=CONTAINER_CPU_LIMIT,
            REDACTED,
            REDACTED,
            network=CONTAINER_NETWORK,
        )
    )
except Exception as e:
    logger.error("Failed to create container manager: %s", e)
    container_manager = None  # type: ignore[assignment]

services:
  bifrost:
    image: maximhq/bifrost:latest
    container_name: bifrost
    ports:
      - "${BIFROST_PORT:-8081}:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./bifrost/data:/app/data
      - ./bifrost/config.json:/app/data/config.json
    env_file:
      - backend/.env
    environment:
      APP_HOST: "0.0.0.0"
    networks:
      - agent-sandbox
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-q", "-O", "/dev/null", "http://localhost:8080/health"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
    restart: unless-stopped

  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: backend/Dockerfile
      args:
        APP_UID: ${APP_UID:-1000}
    image: duckdb-data-agent:latest
    container_name: duckdb-data-agent
    ports:
      - "${APP_PORT:-10000}:10000"
    env_file:
      - backend/.env
    environment:
      CONTAINER_IMAGE: duckdb-agent-sidecar:latest
      CONTAINER_NETWORK: agent-sandbox
      BIFROST_BASE_URL: http://bifrost:8080
      BACKEND_BASE_URL: http://duckdb-data-agent:10000
      SKILLS_DIR: /app/skills
      SKILLS_HOST_PATH: ${SKILLS_HOST_PATH:-${PWD}/skills}
      PLUGINS_HOST_PATH: ${PLUGINS_HOST_PATH:-${PWD}/plugins}
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - ./skills:/app/skills
      - ./plugins:/app/plugins:ro
      - ./data:/app/data
    group_add:
      - "${DOCKER_GID:-0}"
    networks:
      - agent-sandbox
    depends_on:
      bifrost:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  sidecar:
    build:
      context: ./sidecar
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    image: duckdb-agent-sidecar:latest
    profiles:
      - sidecar
    # Never started directly — exists only so `docker compose build`
    # produces the sidecar image. The app spawns sidecar containers
    # on-demand via Docker SDK.

networks:
  agent-sandbox:
    name: agent-sandbox
    external: true

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

BIFROST_BASE_URL = os.getenv("BIFROST_BASE_URL", "http://bifrost:8080")
BACKEND_BASE_URL = os.getenv("BACKEND_BASE_URL", "http://duckdb-data-agent:10000")


def parse_model(value: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Parse 'real_model@sdk_alias' -> (sdk_alias, real_model).

    If no '@', returns (value, value) for backwards compatibility.
    """
    if "@" in value:
        real, sdk = value.rsplit("@", 1)
        return sdk, real
    return value, value


def build_model_rewrites(pairs: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Build a rewrite map from (sdk_alias, real_model) pairs.

    Only includes entries where sdk != real (i.e. rewriting is needed).
    """
    return {sdk: real for sdk, real in pairs if sdk != real}


_raw_model = os.getenv("ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL", "claude-sonnet-4-6")
_raw_sql = os.getenv("SQL_SUBAGENT_MODEL", "inherit")

ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL_SDK, ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL_REAL = parse_model(_raw_model)
SQL_SUBAGENT_MODEL_SDK, SQL_SUBAGENT_MODEL_REAL = parse_model(_raw_sql)

MODEL_REWRITES = build_model_rewrites([
    (ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL_SDK, ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL_REAL),
    (SQL_SUBAGENT_MODEL_SDK, SQL_SUBAGENT_MODEL_REAL),
])

DEFAULT_TOOL_MODEL = parse_model(os.getenv("DEFAULT_TOOL_MODEL", ""))[1]

LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY = os.getenv("LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY", "")
LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY = os.getenv("LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY", "")
LANGFUSE_BASE_URL = os.getenv("LANGFUSE_BASE_URL", "https://cloud.langfuse.com")
LANGFUSE_ENABLED = bool(LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY and LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY)

PROJECT_DIR = os.getenv("PROJECT_DIR", os.getcwd())

## Design Section 1: Architecture Overview

**Current architecture:**
```
Frontend → Backend (FastAPI) → [Docker SDK] → Sidecar Container (Agent SDK)
                              ↓
                         MCP SSE (/mcp)
```

**Proposed architecture:**
```
Frontend → Backend (FastAPI) → [OpenSandbox SDK] → OpenSandbox Server → Sidecar Container
                              ↓                         ↓
                         MCP SSE (/mcp)           Docker or K8s runtime
```

Key changes:
- **Backend** replaces direct Docker SDK calls with OpenSandbox Python SDK (`opensandbox` package)
- **OpenSandbox Server** runs as a separate service, manages container lifecycle via Docker or K8s
- **Sidecar image** stays the same — OpenSandbox just creates/manages the container
- **Backend → Sidecar communication** unchanged: still HTTP POST to `/query` endpoint
- **New config**: `SANDBOX_RUNTIME=docker|kubernetes` to select runtime

The OpenSandbox server handles what `ContainerManager` does today (create, stop, cleanup, shutdown) plus adds K8s support, better security defaults, and the execd health monitoring.
